name: Yara Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Full, but happy. I'm doing computer science, and I live at home with my parents and my two younger sisters in a flat in the part of town where everyone knows everyone. I'm on campus Monday to Thursday, and on Friday evenings and Sunday mornings I work in the kitchen of a care home, serving meals and washing up. Sundays after that I go to church, where I help with the youth group, and then there's a big family lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Is it unusual in your family to go to university?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, I'm the first. My mother cleans and my father drives a taxi, and they're proud, but they don't really understand what I do all day. My aunt tells everyone I'm going to build robots. I try to explain that mostly it's typing and thinking, and my little sister laughs and says that sounds boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine with me, because I've never believed these machines could do everything. I'd tell my friends at church that people still matter, and that what counts is how you treat each other. At the care home they're trying a tablet for ordering meals, and the cook says it's slower than writing it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thankful, but I wouldn't be at ease. We live carefully at home. If my father's taxi work slows down, or my mother loses a cleaning client, I notice at once, and that's whether or not AI changes anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on: study, my shifts, and the youth group. I'd give my mother a bit of my wages every month for the household, like I do now. And I'd ask the care home if I can get an extra shift in the holidays, because I'd like to graduate with less debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, grateful. But I'd keep one ear open for what's happening at home, because that's what really decides my mood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, my father's car is old and he's saving for a new one. If my father's taxi breaks down for a month, we'd skip meals, and no news about AI would help with that. So I'm careful with what I spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes, to understand a coding error, or to check my English. I don't trust it with anything important. My lecturer says to treat it like a classmate who sometimes makes things up.

say: I'd say it's fine with me; I never believed machines could do **everything**.
I'd tell friends at church that how you treat each other still **counts**.
think: I'd be thankful, but at home a slow month for **dad's taxi** would be felt at once.
What decides my mood is **home**, not AI.
do: Carry on with study, shifts and the **youth group**.
Give mum some of my **wages** each month.
Ask the care home for an extra **holiday** shift.
feel: **Calm** and grateful, with one ear on what's happening at home.
S0.quote: If my father's taxi breaks down for a month, we'd skip meals, and no news about AI would help with that
fieldNote: Her unease comes from **dad's old taxi** and mum's cleaning clients, not AI.
She hands part of her **wages** to the household every month.
She uses AI **sometimes**, treating it like a classmate who makes things up.

steps.text: Keep the Friday and Sunday care home shifts
Give mum a fixed part of my wages each month
Ask the care home for extra shifts in the holidays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard on some and good for others, and that we should look after each other either way. I'd tell my friends that people who prepare calmly will be fine, and the ones who panic will make bad decisions. At church I'd probably say we should help the older people learn the new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried, because writing and coding are on the card, and that's my course. But I'd also feel that I've got time and I'm learning. The people I'd worry about are my parents, because cleaning and driving are the sort of jobs that change after, but not right away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for a placement or internship, and I'd learn the AI tools properly, because they're clearly part of work now. I'd join a student group for women in tech, because I'd rather go in with friends. And I'd keep the care home shifts, because that sort of work always needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix. Hopeful, because I believe things work out if you work, but also cautious. I can feel the pressure for me to be the one who sorts it out for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does that pressure fall on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm first in the family to go to university, so everyone expects me to land something well paid. My parents saved and sacrificed so I could study, and I can't say that the plan might not work out. I'd feel I was letting them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sisters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To keep learning, to be kind, and to try new things without being scared. And not to count on one job for life. I'd say that from the kitchen at the care home as I'm washing up.

say: I'd say it's going to be hard on some and good for others, so **look after each other**.
I'd tell friends calm preparation beats **panic**.
think: I'm worried since coding and writing are on the card, but I've got **time**.
The pressure to land something well paid for the **family** sits on me.
do: Aim for a **placement** and learn the AI tools properly.
Join a student group for **women in tech**.
Keep the **care home** shifts, since that work always needs people.
feel: **Hopeful** but cautious, with pressure to sort it out for the family.
S1.quote: My parents saved and sacrificed so I could study, and I can't say that the plan might not work out
fieldNote: Her **family** expects her to land a well-paid job, which adds to the pressure.
She picks **care work** as a steady fallback income.
She looks for **community**, such as a women-in-tech group.

steps.text: Learn one AI coding tool properly this term
Apply for an internship through the women in tech group
Join the women in tech student group
Keep the care home shifts through the year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and I'd pray about it and ask my family to pray. I'd tell my sisters not to worry, because I'd want them to feel safe, but I'd also say we should look after each other. At church I'd probably ask whether the community could help families who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be very afraid. The thinking work I'm studying for would be done by AI before I graduate, and I'm the one my family counts on. I'd feel the weight of the sacrifices they've made, and I'd think the degree might have been for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the university and the church for advice, and I'd think about moving to something hands-on and caring, like nursing or care work, where people still want a human. I'd take every extra shift at the care home, and put what I earn into a family fund. I'd also talk with my father about whether the taxi could be shared with another family driver, to cover costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, like I couldn't breathe. I'd go to the prayer meeting and I'd cry a bit, because there isn't anyone else I'd show it to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, because they would find out anyway. I'd tell my mum and dad that I may need to change my degree, and that it's not their fault or mine. I'd rather say it than carry it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the delay in robots help care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Care work needs touch and patience, and I think robots will take longer there. But I wouldn't be sure, and the care home might still replace the kitchen staff first. I'd be thinking of Magda, who works with me.

say: I'd say it's **frightening**, and I'd pray and ask my family to pray.
I'd ask whether the church could **help** families who lose work.
think: I'd be very afraid: the work I'm studying for would be done by **AI** before I graduate.
The degree might have been for **nothing**, and my family counts on me.
do: Ask the university and **church** for advice.
Consider a switch to **nursing or care work**, where people want a human.
Take every extra **shift** and put pay into a family fund.
feel: **Heavy**, like I couldn't breathe, with only prayer meetings to cry in.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum and dad that I may need to change my degree, and that it's not their fault or mine
fieldNote: Her fear is amplified by being the **first** in the family at university.
She turns to **care work** as the human-touch fallback.
She plans to tell her **parents** the truth early.

steps.text: Ask the university about switching to a nursing degree
Take every extra care home shift I'm offered
Ask the church for help with advice and contacts
Put my pay into a family emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is enough to do something sensible, as long as we start. I'd tell my friends at church that families and communities need to plan together. I'd also say we should be fair to people who lose out, because it isn't their fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more hopeful than with two years. I'd finish the degree and get a couple of years' experience. I'd be 23, and the loan would be there, but I'd have a chance to build a base before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get an internship, and learn to work with the AI tools. I'd also stay close to the care home, maybe train as a care assistant on weekends as a fallback. And I'd save for my sisters' schooling, because I'd like them to have an easier road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, with a little sadness. It's the sort of news that makes me look at my sisters differently, like I want to protect them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a fallback in care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen how much people need someone who shows up. A machine can bring a meal to a room, but only a person can sit with an old woman who's frightened of the night. I'd like to be able to do that if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have less choice. I'd go for care work earlier and drop the degree if I had to. With five years, I can finish and keep both options.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to do something sensible if we start.
I'd say we should be **fair** to people who lose out.
think: I'd feel more **hopeful** than with two years: I'd have time to build a base.
I'd be 23 with a **loan**, but with a chance to prepare.
do: Finish the degree, get an **internship** and learn the AI tools.
Train as a **care assistant** on weekends as a fallback.
feel: **Steady**, with some sadness and a wish to protect my sisters.
S3.quote: A machine can bring a meal to a room, but only a person can sit with an old woman who's frightened of the night
fieldNote: Five years lets her keep **both** options, the degree and care work.
She frames care work as **human presence**, not just a job.

steps.text: Apply for an internship in second year
Train as a care assistant on weekends
Save for my sisters' school costs from my wages
Talk to my parents about their plans each Sunday lunch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth and last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a generous gift, and we should use it well. I'd tell my friends we should build a community that supports everyone, not just the ones who adapt quickly. At church I'd say it's a chance to make sure no one is left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quite peaceful about my own future. By 28 I'd likely have a good job, savings and maybe a family. What I'd think about is my parents, who'd be near sixty, and my sisters, who'd be finishing school as it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a few years, and save more than I spend. I'd keep volunteering with the youth group, and I'd learn the AI tools that change the work I do. I'd also help my parents buy a better car, and keep some money for my sisters' training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, grateful and a bit responsible. Ten years feels like a season I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope the youth group gets from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd tell the teenagers at church that the world is changing, and that being kind and learning something real will still count in ten years. That's what I hope they take from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think ten years would really be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope so, but I'd still put money aside. I trust people to adjust, but I don't trust the timetable.

say: I'd say ten years is a **generous gift**, and we should use it well.
I'd say it's a chance to make sure **no one** is left behind.
think: I'd be **peaceful** about my own future: a job, savings and maybe a family by 28.
I'd think about my **parents** and sisters as it lands.
do: Finish the degree, work a few years and **save** more than I spend.
Help my parents buy a better **car**.
S4.quote: I'd tell the teenagers at church that the world is changing, and that being kind and learning something real will still count in ten years
fieldNote: Ten years leaves her **peaceful** about herself while her family stays on her mind.
She sees the youth group as a place to pass on **calm**.
She still keeps **money aside**, since she distrusts the timetable.

steps.text: Save more than I spend in the first working years
Help my parents buy a safer, newer taxi
Learn the AI tools that change my own work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it gives my family no time to prepare, and I'm the one they're counting on. What would help is clear support for families, like help with study costs and a promise that the community won't be left behind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as strong as I look. My parents think I'm the one who has it all worked out, but I'm learning as I go, one week at a time. I'd like someone to tell students that's okay.

headlineQuote: My parents think I'm the one who has it all worked out, but I'm learning as I go, one week at a time
portrait: Yara is an **18-year-old** computer science first-year, the first in her family to go to university.
She is traditional and steady, lives with parents and two sisters, and works in a care home kitchen.
Her mother cleans and her father drives a taxi, so she watches **family money** closely.
She turns to faith, community and care work as supports and as a fallback.
Her mood runs from uneasy to alarmed at two years, easing to calm with ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most, because her family would have no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **support** for families, such as help with study costs, and no one left behind.
